title: Landmark keys in DRAM, full KV blocks indexed on flash
idea: Inverts 'attention needs every past token resident': DRAM keeps one landmark key per 64-token block, and the full KV blocks sit on NVMe/CXL flash. Each decode step fetches only the top-k blocks whose landmarks score highest against the query.
why: Million-token contexts need DRAM for only ~2-5% of their KV: a 20-50x cut in KV DRAM.
note: Landmark/Quest-style top-k block retrieval puts 95%+ of long-context KV on flash; widely pursued, so low novelty.

title: Rank/select engines enabling succinct trees and graphs in DRAM
idea: Information theory says an n-node tree needs only ~2n bits, yet pointer trees spend ~128n. Add rank/select and balanced-parentheses navigation units next to the memory controller so succinct encodings (LOUDS, BP, Elias-Fano adjacency lists) traverse in O(1) per hop at near-pointer speed.
why: 5-20x smaller indexes, tries, graphs and genomics structures, which are often DRAM-bound.

title: Compiler swaps pointer structures for succinct ones with rank/select instructions
idea: IFR: indexes sized at the information-theoretic minimum. Closest: a profile-guided compiler pass replaces read-mostly maps, sets and trees with succinct equivalents (Elias-Fano, wavelet trees, compressed tries) backed by new rank/select instructions.
why: 2-5x footprint cut for indexes and graphs in search, ads and genomics.

title: Sodium spikes: streaming transformers store only the KV that fires
idea: Like a neuron's Na+ action potential that fires only past threshold, a video/audio streaming model compares each new frame's token KV with the co-located token of the previous frame and stores a new entry only if the change exceeds a learned per-layer threshold; unchanged tokens become 2-byte back-references.
why: Static-camera, screen and speech streams repeat 70-95% of tokens frame to frame; KV for long streaming contexts shrinks 5-20x (density, cost/bit).
note: Temporal token reduction for video LLMs is an active area; per-layer thresholding a twist.

title: Ternary weights packed five trits per byte with LUT decode
idea: Box: representation shrink × model training × weights × train time × 3^5 = 243 states in 8 bits + table decode. Models trained natively ternary store five weights per byte and decode via a 256-entry table held in registers or shared memory.
why: 1.6 bits per weight versus 16 is a 10× weight-memory cut, achieved with algorithms and existing GPUs only, so no fluorinated chemistry.

title: Keyword-spotter extreme: ternary weights stored as zero-skipping trit runs
idea: From always-on keyword spotters that run ternary networks: models are trained to {-1, 0, +1} weights stored as base-3 packed trits (5 per byte) with run-length skip lists for zeros, decoded by adder-only compute units that skip zero runs.
why: About 1.6 bits per weight or less versus 16 is a 10x+ cut in weight DRAM/HBM, and fab water falls proportionally.

title: Map-tile mipmaps: multi-resolution embeddings split across DRAM and flash
idea: Like web maps loading coarse tiles before fine ones, store a 4-bit coarse version of each embedding or retrieval vector in DRAM and its residual refinement levels on flash; the model uses the coarse level by default and fetches residuals only when a confidence check fails.
why: Most lookups are satisfied at the coarse level; ~4x less DRAM for large embedding and retrieval indexes with flash serving <10% of reads.

title: Dictionary: fleet-trained compression dictionaries pinned per workload
idea: Train zstd-style dictionaries per workload class (JVM heaps, Python objects, embeddings) from fleet samples, ship them signed with the binary, and pin them in the hardware compressor's SRAM so even single 4 KB pages compress against a rich shared context.
why: Small-page ratio rises from ~2x to 3x or more, making zswap/hardware compressed tiers 30-50% more effective at saving DRAM.

title: JPEG for the KV cache: DCT along the token axis
idea: Treat each attention head's K and V as an image (tokens x channels), apply a block DCT along the token axis where neighbouring tokens correlate, and quantize with per-head learned quantization tables like JPEG luminance tables; the attention kernel inverse-transforms blocks in SRAM.
why: KV cache dominates long-context inference memory; transform coding before quantization claims 4-8x smaller KV at <1% quality loss vs ~2-4x for plain quantization.

title: Via-programmed mask ROM holding year-frozen foundation model weights
idea: A standard base die, built on a DRAM-periphery or mature logic process, adds one contact/via mask that encodes a frozen model's weights as present or absent vias. Each bit takes about 2-4 F^2 and needs no capacitor and no refresh. The dies stack HBM-style beside the accelerator, and each new model release costs just that one mask. The time-scale insight: weights stay unchanged for 6-18 months, so they need no rewritable cells.
why: Weights (30-60% of inference HBM) leave DRAM entirely. A ROM bit costs about 3x less than a DRAM bit and needs no refresh energy, all for one added mask per model version.
note: One added via mask moves frozen weights out of HBM, no refresh; doubt is model churn vs 6-18 month freeze and Taalas-style prior art.

title: Teletext data carousel: broadcast weights to accelerators that store nothing
idea: Borrowed from broadcast TV data carousels that loop content for any receiver to catch: a rack-level weight server streams the model layer by layer in a continuous optical multicast loop from ROM/NAND, and every accelerator computes on each layer as it passes, aligning its batches to the carousel phase.
why: N accelerators share one non-volatile copy of weights with zero weight DRAM and zero refresh; per-accelerator DRAM shrinks to KV only.
note: N accelerators share one streamed weight copy; doubt: batch-phase alignment and latency, Cerebras-style weight streaming partly known.

title: Monk with one bowl: eBPF census finds duplicate buffer copies
idea: A monk owns one bowl, not five. An eBPF plus page-hash census tool samples contents across the page cache, socket buffers, user heaps and GPU staging buffers and flags identical data held in two or more places (the NIC-kernel-user-serialize-GPU chain). The team then ships upstream zero-copy patches (io_uring registered buffers, splice, mmap'd page cache) for the top offenders.
why: Data-path services hold 2-5 copies of in-flight data. A small team can free 10-25% of DRAM on storage, proxy and ingest nodes.
